taxonomyNote: NatureServe notes the taxonomy of this complex is controversial: some authors recognize from two to eleven or more species, others treat it as one.
fieldMarks: Slender, small salamander: total length up to about 120 mm (BC).
Uniform pinkish brown, often with a yellow tinge at the base of the legs and digits; yellow or brown flecks sometimes on the sides (BC).
Large head and eyes, relatively long limbs, and a narrow constriction at the tail base that can be hard to see in small animals (BC).
Hatchlings are black or dark gray mottled with lighter flecks, with bright yellow leg bases (BC).
behavior: Lives entirely on the forest floor from egg to adult; no aquatic larval stage, young hatch as miniature adults (BC; NatureServe).
Sheltering under or inside rotting logs, stumps, bark piles, rodent burrows or moist crevices (BC).
Eats insects, spiders and millipedes; inactive in cold or hot dry weather, emerging with fall rains and active until about May or June in the north and at high elevations (NatureServe).
Female broods a cluster of 7-25 eggs, which hatch in fall or early winter (NatureServe).
habitat: Douglas-fir and maple forest and clearings in the north; redwood forest, chaparral, oak woodland and canyons on the coast; pine-oak-incense cedar forest in the Sierra Nevada (NatureServe).
range: Southwestern British Columbia south along the Coast Ranges to northwestern Baja California, and on the western slopes of the Cascades and Sierra Nevada; absent from the Sacramento-San Joaquin valley; sea level to about 8,000 ft (NatureServe). North of the Sunshine Coast it is known from only a few isolated sites in British Columbia (BC).
